subject: Accounting
title: Reconciliation and Review
description: A 60-second lesson on Reconciliation and Review.

hook.text: The bank says you have $50,000. Your books say $52,000. That $2,000 gap needs explaining.

buildup.text: Reconciliation compares two sets of records to find and resolve differences.

discovery.text: Monthly bank reconciliations catch errors, unauthorized transactions, and timing differences.

twist.text: Skipping reconciliation is one of the most common ways small frauds go undetected for years.

climax.text: Management review adds a second layer—someone senior examines key accounts for reasonableness.

punchline.text: Reconcile early, reconcile often. Gaps grow fast.

quiz.question: What does bank reconciliation accomplish?
options: It finds differences between bank records and company books
It eliminates the need for audits

details.summary: Reconciliation compares two sets of records to ensure they agree — like matching bank statements to internal ledgers — while analytical review compares financial data against expectations to identify unusual patterns that warrant investigation.
details.whyItMatters: Reconciliation and review are the workhorses of financial accuracy, catching errors and anomalies that would otherwise compound over time and corrupt financial statements.
takeaways: Bank reconciliation matches company records to bank statements, identifying timing differences and errors
Analytical review compares financial results to budgets, prior periods, and industry benchmarks
Unexplained variances from analytical review are red flags that trigger further investigation

faq.question: What is a bank reconciliation?
faq.answer: A bank reconciliation matches the company's internal cash records to its bank statement. Differences arise from timing (outstanding checks, deposits in transit) and errors. Regular reconciliation ensures all transactions are properly recorded and identifies unauthorized activity quickly.

faq.question: How does analytical review help auditors?
faq.answer: Auditors compare current financial data to expectations — prior year results, budgets, industry averages. If revenue jumped 40% while the industry grew 3%, that demands explanation. Analytical review efficiently highlights areas that need deeper investigation without testing every transaction.
